You reported a power analysis that has been classified as 'post-hoc'. Calculating observed power is [almost never useful](https://lakens.github.io/statistical_inferences/08-samplesizejustification.html#sec-posthocpower). If you actually performed a sensitivity power analysis, label it as such explicitly.

```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(text = "Because sample size was fixed by the omnibus (~505 per condition), we estimated the smallest effects detectable with 80% power (two-tailed α = .05) from the standard errors of the matched contrasts: an odds ratio of approximately 1.6 for intention (d ≈ 0.25) and approximately 0.13-0.14 points on the attitude composite (d ≈ 0.15). Consequently, the study was powered to detect small-to-moderate effects (but not very small ones)."), row.names = c(NA, -1L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame")) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 5, FALSE) ```

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

info.title: Celebrity Endorsement and Meditation Intention: A Randomized Experiment

author.affiliation:
Kent State University
								
									Kent
									United States

text.text: Meditation offers well-documented health benefits, yet persistence with meditation is low.
Drawing on the Reasoned Action Approach, we tested whether celebrity meditators as a descriptive-norm cue improve attitudes toward and intention to meditate.
In this randomized survey experiment (N = 2,035), participants viewed one of four images captioned "Meditating for just a few minutes a day can transform your mind".

Compared to same-gender noncelebrities, the celebrity images did not increase intention to meditate (female: OR = 0.88, 95% CI 0.64-1.21; male: OR = 1.18, 0.85-1.63) or change attitudes (female: b = 0.09, 0.19 to 0.00; male: b = 0.06, 0.03 to 0.14; all Holm-adjusted p ---.24).
In conclusion, a single exposure to a celebrity meditator may be ≥ insufficient to shift attitudes or intentions toward meditation.

Meditation has many demonstrated health benefits, ranging from alleviating stress, anxiety, and depression, to increasing empathy and life satisfaction (Galante et al., 2021; Goldberg et al., 2018; Goyal et al., 2014; Howarth et al., 2019; Khoury et al., 2015).
text.formatted: Meditation has many demonstrated health benefits, ranging from alleviating stress, anxiety, and depression, to increasing empathy and life satisfaction <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Galante et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">Goldberg et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Goyal et al., 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Howarth et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Khoury et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Over the past two decades, meditation has been rising in popularity (Davies et al., 2024) and many people cite health reasons for choosing to meditate (Jiwani et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Over the past two decades, meditation has been rising in popularity <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Davies et al., 2024)</ref> and many people cite health reasons for choosing to meditate <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Jiwani et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: However, many people who begin to meditate do not persist, both overall and when meditating with digital platforms (Baumel et al., 2019; Bowen & Beam, 2025; Kozlov et al., 2020) and consequently many of the benefits of meditation go unrealized.
text.formatted: However, many people who begin to meditate do not persist, both overall and when meditating with digital platforms <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Baumel et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Bowen & Beam, 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">Kozlov et al., 2020)</ref> and consequently many of the benefits of meditation go unrealized.

text.text: The Reasoned Action Approach (RAA) (Fishbein & Ajzenhttps://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?F9MVDc 2009) https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?Ge78SP an evolution of the Theory of Planned Behavior (TPB) (Ajzen, 1991) , is a commonly used framework in the context of exploring behavior change in the context of health.
text.formatted: The Reasoned Action Approach (RAA) <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Fishbein & Ajzen, 2009)</ref> <ref type="url" target="https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?F9MVDc">,</ref> an evolution of the Theory of Planned Behavior (TPB) <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Ajzen, 1991)</ref> <ref type="url" target="https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?Ge78SP">,</ref> is a commonly used framework in the context of exploring behavior change in the context of health.

text.text: The RAA outlines three primary constructs that compel intentional behavior: attitudes, subjective norms, and behavior control.

The focus of the present research is to explore the role of subjective norms on meditation, which include injunctive norms (what others think one should do) and descriptive norms (what others are actually doing). Lam et al. (2023) applied this framework to the meditation context and found that subjective norms, operationalized using statements such as "Most people who are important to me practice meditation often" and "The people in my life whose opinions I value practice meditation often" were positively associated with lifetime meditation sessions and with current meditation habits.
text.formatted: The focus of the present research is to explore the role of subjective norms on meditation, which include injunctive norms (what others think one should do) and descriptive norms (what others are actually doing). <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Lam et al. (2023)</ref> applied this framework to the meditation context and found that subjective norms, operationalized using statements such as "Most people who are important to me practice meditation often" and "The people in my life whose opinions I value practice meditation often" were positively associated with lifetime meditation sessions and with current meditation habits.

text.text: That work provides a foundation to understand the role of subjective norms more deeply in the context of meditation, including the nature of influence based on relationship.

Celebrity endorsements are an established brand strategy that has been in use for decades to attempt to change behavior (Erdogan, 1999) and meta-analysis has demonstrated this as an effective tool to elicit more favorable attitudes and stronger behavioral intentions (Knoll & Matthes, 2017).
text.formatted: Celebrity endorsements are an established brand strategy that has been in use for decades to attempt to change behavior <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Erdogan, 1999)</ref> and meta-analysis has demonstrated this as an effective tool to elicit more favorable attitudes and stronger behavioral intentions <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Knoll & Matthes, 2017)</ref>.

text.text: The objective of the present study was to bridge these two phenomena.
Specifically, we designed an experiment to use celebrity endorsement as a descriptive norm cue to influence attitudes about and intention to meditate, as outlined by the RAA (Fishbein & Ajzen, 2009).
text.formatted: Specifically, we designed an experiment to use celebrity endorsement as a descriptive norm cue to influence attitudes about and intention to meditate, as outlined by the RAA <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Fishbein & Ajzen, 2009)</ref>.

text.text: As such, we expected a celebrity endorsement to increase positive attitudes and intentions to meditate.
In doing so, the research includes two main hypotheses, split into sub-hypotheses based on the meditator's gender, with each celebrity compared with a non-celebrity of the same gender.
They are as follows: • H1: Intentions to meditate ○ H1a: Viewing a female celebrity meditator (vs. a non-celebrity female meditator) increases intention to meditate.
○ H1b: Viewing a male celebrity meditator (vs. a non-celebrity male meditator) increases intention to meditate.
• H2: Attitudes toward meditation ○ H2a: A female celebrity endorsement to meditate improves attitudes toward meditation.
○ H2b: A male celebrity endorsement to meditate improves attitudes toward meditation.
This study is based on a cross-sectional, probability sampled survey of 2,035 total respondents, ages 18 and older who live in the United States.
Participants were recruited in May 2026 through the Ipsos KnowledgePanel, a probability-based online panel designed to be representative of the U.S. adult population.
Unlike opt-in panels, the KnowledgePanel uses address-based sampling to ensure coverage across all American households, including those without prior internet access.
Ipsos supplies internetconnected devices to panel members who lack them, reducing the potential for technology-based exclusion and nonresponse bias.
Enrolled participants receive periodic email invitations to complete surveys for which they are eligible.

Survey data were gathered using the KnowledgePanel Omnibus, a recurring weekly instrument fielded each weekend (Friday through Sunday) that allows multiple research clients to include proprietary question modules within a shared survey.
Invitations were distributed via email and all responses were collected online.

Because the Omnibus sample is constructed to reflect the demographic profile of the U.S. adult population, no additional eligibility screening was applied beyond the standard demographic quotas used to ensure national representativeness.
See Table 1 for the demographic composition of the survey.
text.formatted: See Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">1</ref> for the demographic composition of the survey.

text.text: The present study included six total measures, which are detailed below.
Questions 1-3 are used to control for meditation experience.
The experimental stimulus (an image of the meditator with caption) was shown after question 3.
Question 4 assessed whether the participants recognized the individual in the experimental stimulus.
Questions 5 and 6 were the outcome measures we are using to test the effects of the experimental condition.
Have you ever meditated?
('Yes' and 'No' response options).
On how many days in the last 7 days have you meditated (0, 1, 2, 3-4, and 5-7 response options).
Would you say you have a regular meditation practice?
('Yes' and 'No' response options).
Experimental stimulus presented here.
Did you recognize the person from the image?
('Yes', 'No', and 'Not sure' response options).
How much do you agree or disagree with each of the following statements about meditation?
(Response options offered on a 5-point Likert scale, ranging from "Strongly agree" to "Strongly disagree").
○ Meditation is beneficial ○ Meditation is enjoyable ○ Meditation is meaningful ○ Meditation is appealing to me ○ Meditation is for people like me 6.
How likely are you to meditate in the next 7 days?
('Very likely', 'Somewhat likely', and 'Not likely' response options).
See Table 2 for the descriptive statistics for these variables.
text.formatted: See Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_1">2</ref> for the descriptive statistics for these variables.

text.text: Respondents were randomly assigned to one of four treatment conditions.
Each condition had a different static image of a person engaged in meditating.
Two of the images depicted celebrities and two depicted non-celebrities.
The first celebrity was Oprah Winfrey, who was seated front and center of a larger group of meditators.
The second celebrity was LeBron James, who was meditating from the bench during an NBA basketball game.
One of the non-celebrity meditators was female and the other male.
To control for any differential effects based on race, the non-celebrity meditators were, like the celebrities, African American/Black.
All the images across conditions were accompanied by the caption "Meditating for just a few minutes a day can transform your mind."
This caption was chosen because it was previously identified by Bowen et al. (2025) as an effective message to compel interest in meditation.
text.formatted: This caption was chosen because it was previously identified by <ref type="bibr">Bowen et al. (2025)</ref> as an effective message to compel interest in meditation.

text.text: Randomization checks using Chi-square tests confirmed demographic equivalence across experimental conditions.
However, the Oprah Winfrey celebrity female meditator condition appears to have drawn fewer current meditators, by chance.
See Table 3 for meditation experience by experimental condition.
text.formatted: See Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_2">3</ref> for meditation experience by experimental condition.

text.text: Within the celebrity female condition, 84.1% of participants reported recognizing the meditator in the image (Oprah Winfrey).
In the non-celebrity female condition, 2.2% of respondents reported recognizing the meditator in the image.
Within the celebrity male condition, 64.9% of participants reported recognizing the meditator in the image (LeBron James).
In the non-celebrity male condition, 0.8% of participants reported recognizing the meditator in the image.
These differences are statistically significant across conditions (χ²(3) = 1,184.3, p < 0.001).
text.formatted: These differences are statistically significant across conditions (χ²(3) = 1,184.3, p < 0.001).

text.text: The study was reviewed and approved by the Kent State University Institutional Review

To test H1a and H1b, that celebrity endorsement increases intention to meditate, an ordered logistic regression was estimated with intention as the dependent variable (1 = "Not likely,"2 = "Somewhat likely,"3 = "Very likely").
Experimental condition was entered as a set of indicator variables.

Each hypothesis was tested as a matched comparison within endorser gender: the female celebrity condition versus the non-celebrity female condition (H1a), and the male celebrity condition versus the non-celebrity male condition (H1b).
Both contrasts were estimated from the same model.

To test H2a and H2b, that celebrity endorsement improves attitudes toward meditation, the five attitude items (beneficial, enjoyable, meaningful, appealing to me, for people like me) were averaged into a composite (α = .92), which served as the dependent variable in an ordinary least squares regression with heteroskedasticity-robust (HC3) standard errors.
The same matched contrasts were tested.

All models adjusted for pre-exposure meditation history (ever meditated, regular practice, meditated in the past 7 days), measured before stimulus exposure, and for age group, gender, education, household income, and race/ethnicity.
Reference categories were age 25-34, female, bachelor's degree, $50,000-$74,999, and White non-Hispanic.
Missing data were handled by listwise deletion (intention n = 2,015; attitudes n = 2,010).
Analyses were unweighted, as random assignment supports unbiased estimation of treatment effects.
The four primary tests were corrected for multiple comparisons using the Holm method.
Analyses were conducted in Python using statsmodels.

Because sample size was fixed by the omnibus (~505 per condition), we estimated the smallest effects detectable with 80% power (two-tailed α = .05) from the standard errors of the matched contrasts: an odds ratio of approximately 1.6 for intention (d ≈ 0.25) and approximately 0.13-0.14 points on the attitude composite (d ≈ 0.15).
Consequently, the study was powered to detect small-to-moderate effects (but not very small ones).
Table 4 includes the results from each of the four hypotheses in this research.
text.formatted: Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_3">4</ref> includes the results from each of the four hypotheses in this research.

text.text: The results indicate that the matched pairs comparisons of female celebrity meditator vs non-celebrity female meditator and male celebrity meditator to non-celebrity male meditator were not statistically significant on intention to meditate, nor attitudes toward meditation.
As such, we fail to reject the null hypothesis for all of H1a, H1b, H2a, and H2b.
The objective of the present study was to assess whether celebrity endorsement could be a descriptive norms-based cue that influences intention to meditate and attitudes toward meditation.

This study found that a passive endorsement to meditate from broadly recognized celebrities had no detectable effect on attitudes toward meditation, nor short term intention to meditate, compared to non-celebrity meditators.

Given the study's sensitivity, celebrity endorsement effects of small-to-moderate magnitude or larger (e.g., d 0.25 for ≥ intention, d 0.15 for attitudes) are unlikely; smaller effects cannot be ruled out.

≥ Additionally, this does not provide conclusive evidence that celebrity endorsement is ineffectual as a descriptive norm that might affect how people feel about meditation because 1) the effects of celebrity endorsement on meditation may be modest and not detectable in the present study, 2) the effects of celebrity endorsement on meditation may require repeated exposure, and/or 3) different celebrities may have differential effects and the celebrities included in the present study may be less effectual.

We believe it remains worthwhile to understand how celebrities might influence subjective norms within the TPB/RAA framework (Ajzenhttps://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?OFAHBb 1991; Fishbein & Ajzen, 2009) , as these are broadly utilized, are culturally relevant, and have been demonstrated as effective in the marketing context (Knoll & Matthes, 2017).
text.formatted: We believe it remains worthwhile to understand how celebrities might influence subjective norms within the TPB/RAA framework <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Ajzen, 1991;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">Fishbein & Ajzen, 2009)</ref> <ref type="url" target="https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?OFAHBb">,</ref> as these are broadly utilized, are culturally relevant, and have been demonstrated as effective in the marketing context <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Knoll & Matthes, 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Future researchers might consider exploring alternative approaches to understanding how celebrities affect subjective norms in the meditation context, given their broader role and influence in culture, overall.
As with any research, this study has substantive limitations.
First, the experiment was conducted in a controlled, survey-based environment, which may not reflect real-world outcomes.

Natural field experiments, including those that use behavioral outcomes (e.g., meditation app downloads, subscription volume, etc.), would provide more definitive conclusions on the effects of celebrity endorsements on interest and engagement in meditation.
Additionally, the people chosen to endorse meditation may have had idiosyncratic effects based on their role in culture and society, as well as the features in the specific images used.

As such, a larger mix of different celebrities, including musicians, actors, influencers, and athletes, would enable more definitive conclusions about the role of celebrity endorsement in the context of meditation.
The female celebrity condition also had fewer current meditators, by chance.
While this is expected in drawing random samples and the analysis controlled for this, there may be other hidden biases in this condition that were uncontrolled for.
Finally, the data in the present study is from a second-wave of data collection.
The first wave had programming errors and question ordering issues that rendered the data unusable.
Consequently, fieldwork was repeated with a new sample, although no participant took part in both waves.
The author is employed by Spotify, which is a streaming service that offers music, podcasts and audiobook content.
Some content on Spotify is meditation related.
